The Kreutzer Sonata. Leo Tolstoy's The Kreutzer Sonata is a dark meditation on marriage, jealousy, and sexual desire, told through a passenger's monologue confessing to his wife's murder. A man on a train reveals to a stranger that he has killed his wife, then narrates the deterioration of his marriage from its passionate beginning to its tragic end. He describes the spiritual deadness that follows sexual consummation, the erosion of tenderness, and the resentment born from treating marriage as a duty. The turning point arrives when a musician begins regularly visiting to play Beethoven's Kreutzer Sonata with his wife, and the narrator becomes convinced of an affair. Tolstoy uses the Sonata as a metaphor for the dangerous power of art and sensuality to stir passion and destroy domestic stability. The narrator's obsession with the music, his wife's apparent intimacy with the musician, and his simmering rage create an atmosphere of mounting crisis. He murders his wife in a fit of jealous rage, but the novella never entirely clarifies whether the affair was real or imagined—the narrator's perspective is inherently unreliable. The work is simultaneously a confession, a philosophical argument against sexual relationships, and an exploration of masculine violence and paranoia, making it one of his most controversial and psychologically intense works.
